questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Diphenhydramine on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: First-generation H1 antihistamine
Second-generation H1 antihistamine
Leukotriene receptor antagonist
Nonopioid antitussive

questions.rationale: Diphenhydramine is the listed prototype for First-generation H1 antihistamine.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Diphenhydramine?

options.text: Blocks central and peripheral H1 receptors, including receptors in the brain
Blocks peripheral H1 receptors with minimal entry into the brain
Blocks airway leukotriene receptors to limit mucus production
Blocks airway muscarinic receptors to limit bronchoconstriction

questions.rationale: Blocks H1 receptors and crosses the blood-brain barrier. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client becomes sleepy after taking diphenhydramine. Which explanation best fits this response?

options.text: The drug crosses the blood-brain barrier and blocks CNS H1 receptors
The drug remains mainly peripheral and reduces alertness through low blood pressure
The drug suppresses the medullary cough center through an opioid action
The drug enhances the inhibitory effects of GABA in the brain

questions.rationale: Diphenhydramine crosses the blood-brain barrier and commonly causes drowsiness. The H1 mechanism distinguishes this response from opioid cough suppression and benzodiazepine-related GABA enhancement.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client starting diphenhydramine plans to drive to work. Which teaching is most appropriate?

options.text: Avoid driving until the medication's effects on alertness are known
Take it with breakfast so the meal will prevent impairment while driving
Wait until the allergy symptoms improve, then judge whether driving is safe
Use the usual driving routine if this dose relieved the allergy symptoms

questions.rationale: Sedation can impair driving and other activities requiring alertness.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which finding in a client taking diphenhydramine is consistent with an anticholinergic effect?

options.text: Difficulty emptying the bladder
Difficulty sleeping through the night
Fine tremor when holding a cup
Loose stools after a meal

questions.rationale: Urinary retention is among the anticholinergic effects of diphenhydramine.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: An older adult reports dizziness after diphenhydramine. Which nursing concern has priority in the care plan?

options.text: Risk for falls
Risk for impaired urinary elimination
Risk for constipation
Risk for impaired oral comfort

questions.rationale: Sedation and impaired alertness increase fall risk, especially in older adults. Other anticholinergic concerns may require monitoring, but dizziness makes immediate fall prevention the priority in this scenario.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client taking diphenhydramine reports dry mouth. Which suggestion matches the course teaching?

options.text: Use sugarless gum or hard candy if safe to swallow
Use an alcohol-containing mouth rinse to manage the sensation of dryness
Take the next dose sooner because dryness suggests inadequate allergy control
Change to another first-generation antihistamine to avoid anticholinergic effects

questions.rationale: Sugarless gum or hard candy can help manage medication-related dry mouth.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which over-the-counter product should a client taking diphenhydramine discuss with the nurse before combining them?

options.text: A nighttime product that also causes drowsiness
A sugarless lozenge intended to relieve a dry mouth
A saline nasal rinse intended to relieve nasal irritation
A nonmedicated nasal strip intended to improve nasal airflow

questions.rationale: Combining CNS depressants can increase sedation; active ingredients should be reviewed. The interaction concern is additive sedation. The other listed nonmedicated measures do not add a CNS depressant.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client taking diphenhydramine develops constipation and blurred vision. How should these findings be interpreted?

options.text: They can reflect the medication's anticholinergic activity
They can reflect increased cholinergic activity
They can reflect beta2-receptor stimulation
They can reflect excessive central dopamine activity

questions.rationale: Constipation and blurred vision are anticholinergic effects, not treatment goals.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which client statement about diphenhydramine requires correction?

options.text: I can have an evening drink if I separate it from the antihistamine dose by an hour
I should check the ingredients in nighttime cold medicines before combining products
I should discuss new urinary hesitancy with the nurse
I should assess my alertness before activities that require balance

questions.rationale: Diphenhydramine enters the CNS; alcohol can worsen its sedative effects. Separating alcohol and diphenhydramine by an hour does not establish that their sedative effects will not overlap.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Cetirizine on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: Second-generation H1 antihistamine
First-generation H1 antihistamine
Leukotriene receptor antagonist
Nonopioid antitussive

questions.rationale: Cetirizine is the listed prototype for Second-generation H1 antihistamine.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Cetirizine?

options.text: Blocks peripheral H1 receptors with relatively little entry into the brain
Blocks central and peripheral H1 receptors with substantial entry into the brain
Blocks leukotriene receptors to limit airway inflammation and mucus
Blocks muscarinic receptors to limit acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction

questions.rationale: Blocks peripheral H1 receptors with less CNS penetration than first-generation agents. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client needs allergy relief during the workday and experienced pronounced sleepiness with diphenhydramine. Which feature supports discussing cetirizine?

options.text: It generally causes less CNS sedation than diphenhydramine
It provides longer beta2 stimulation than diphenhydramine
It suppresses the cough center more directly than diphenhydramine
It blocks muscarinic receptors more strongly than diphenhydramine

questions.rationale: Cetirizine has less CNS penetration and is generally less sedating.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which symptom is an appropriate target when cetirizine is prescribed for seasonal allergies?

options.text: Sneezing associated with seasonal histamine release
Bronchospasm requiring immediate rescue treatment
A dry cough requiring central cough suppression
Airway inflammation requiring inhaled corticosteroid treatment

questions.rationale: Cetirizine is an antihistamine used for allergy symptom control.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client says cetirizine can never cause drowsiness. Which response is best?

options.text: It is less sedating, but check your own response before activities requiring alertness
Its peripheral action means you can judge driving safety from allergy relief alone
Its second-generation classification means food timing determines any drowsiness
Its H1 blockade means the same precautions apply only when it is used at bedtime

questions.rationale: Less sedation does not mean that every client will remain fully alert.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which comparison between cetirizine and diphenhydramine is accurate?

options.text: Cetirizine crosses the blood-brain barrier less readily
Cetirizine blocks leukotrienes rather than histamine
Cetirizine suppresses the central cough reflex more directly
Cetirizine produces stronger central anticholinergic activity

questions.rationale: The course review distinguishes second-generation agents by reduced CNS penetration.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client with seasonal allergies asks whether cetirizine will stop a sudden asthma attack. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: It treats allergies; use the prescribed rescue bronchodilator for sudden bronchospasm
It treats allergies; take it first and reassess before using the rescue bronchodilator
It blocks H1 receptors; that action provides the same rapid airway relief as albuterol
It blocks H1 receptors; that action makes the rescue medicine unnecessary during allergy season

questions.rationale: Cetirizine blocks histamine; it is not a rescue bronchodilator.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which finding would best indicate that cetirizine is achieving the intended allergy benefit?

options.text: Less sneezing and itching without troublesome daytime drowsiness
Less coughing associated with increasing daytime sleepiness
Less wheezing immediately after taking the first tablet
Less need to urinate associated with a drier mouth

questions.rationale: Symptom relief, rather than sedation or urinary retention, is the treatment goal.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client changes from diphenhydramine to cetirizine and asks why the drugs differ in sedation. Which factor is most relevant?

options.text: The extent to which the drug reaches CNS histamine receptors
The extent to which the drug stimulates airway beta2 receptors
The extent to which the drug suppresses medullary cough activity
The extent to which the drug blocks airway leukotriene receptors

questions.rationale: Reduced blood-brain barrier penetration helps explain less sedation with cetirizine.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which client plan after starting cetirizine reflects appropriate caution?

options.text: Observe personal alertness before driving or operating equipment
Judge driving readiness by how quickly sneezing improves after the first dose
Use the usual driving routine because the drug is classified as peripheral acting
Add a bedtime antihistamine routinely to prevent daytime breakthrough symptoms

questions.rationale: Even less-sedating agents warrant attention to individual response and medication combinations.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Codeine on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: Opioid antitussive
Nonopioid antitussive
First-generation H1 antihistamine
Second-generation H1 antihistamine

questions.rationale: Codeine is the listed prototype for Opioid antitussive.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Codeine?

options.text: Suppresses cough through action at the medullary cough center as an opioid
Suppresses cough through a central nonopioid action without analgesic properties
Reduces cough by blocking peripheral histamine H1 receptors
Reduces cough by blocking muscarinic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle

questions.rationale: Suppresses the cough reflex through the medullary cough center. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which assessment is especially important before administering codeine for cough?

options.text: Respiratory rate and breathing quality
Bowel pattern and recent stool consistency
Blood pressure response to position changes
Recent fluid intake and hydration pattern

questions.rationale: Codeine can cause respiratory depression and requires respiratory assessment. Bowel and positional-pressure assessments are also relevant to codeine, but respiratory assessment addresses its most immediate serious safety risk.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client receiving codeine is difficult to arouse and breathing slowly. What is the nurse's priority?

options.text: Assess ventilation immediately and follow emergency and medication-hold procedures
Place the client on fall precautions and complete a routine orthostatic assessment first
Review the last bowel movement and assess the abdomen before addressing the next dose
Ask about cough frequency and document the sedative response before notifying the provider

questions.rationale: Reduced alertness with slow breathing can signal opioid-related respiratory depression.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which teaching helps a client manage constipation associated with codeine when not otherwise restricted?

options.text: Maintain appropriate fluid and fiber intake
Take each dose with food and wait for bowel function to adjust without changing intake
Lower fiber intake temporarily to reduce the effort required for bowel movements
Reduce daytime fluids so fewer position changes are needed while taking the drug

questions.rationale: The course review recommends fluid and fiber to help prevent opioid-related constipation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client feels lightheaded when standing after codeine. Which instruction is appropriate?

options.text: Change positions slowly and obtain help if unsteady
Take the next dose with a larger meal to prevent an opioid-related pressure change
Limit walking for the whole treatment course rather than checking positional symptoms
Change to a seated position quickly and resume standing when the cough improves

questions.rationale: Codeine may cause lightheadedness; slow position changes reduce fall risk.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which client statement about codeine needs follow-up?

options.text: I can take a bedtime sedative with codeine if I separate the doses by an hour
I should check combination cold-product ingredients before adding another medicine
I should ask for help walking if the medication makes me lightheaded
I should discuss constipation if dietary and fluid measures are not helping

questions.rationale: Alcohol and other CNS depressants can increase opioid sedation and respiratory risk. Separating sedating medicines by an hour does not establish a safe combination; review additive CNS-depressant effects first.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client asks why codeine reduced a dry cough without opening narrowed bronchi. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: Its antitussive action suppresses the central cough reflex
It blocks histamine receptors responsible for airway swelling
It blocks leukotriene receptors responsible for airway mucus
It blocks muscarinic receptors responsible for bronchoconstriction

questions.rationale: Codeine suppresses cough centrally; cough suppression is different from bronchodilation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which finding is more concerning than uncomplicated constipation in a client taking codeine?

options.text: New shallow, slowed respirations
New difficulty passing a hard stool
New lightheadedness when rising from bed
New sleepiness while remaining readily arousable

questions.rationale: Respiratory depression can be immediately dangerous and takes priority over routine constipation teaching.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A nurse evaluates a client's response to prescribed codeine for cough. Which finding supports therapeutic benefit without an obvious safety warning?

options.text: Less coughing while remaining readily arousable with adequate breathing
Less coughing accompanied by increasing difficulty staying awake
Less coughing accompanied by lightheadedness during each transfer
Less coughing accompanied by a progressive decline in respiratory rate

questions.rationale: Cough relief must be evaluated together with alertness and respiratory safety. Relief must be accompanied by preserved arousability and adequate breathing, rather than judged from cough suppression alone.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Dextromethorphan on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: Nonopioid antitussive
Opioid antitussive
First-generation H1 antihistamine
Second-generation H1 antihistamine

questions.rationale: Dextromethorphan is the listed prototype for Nonopioid antitussive.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Dextromethorphan?

options.text: Suppresses the medullary cough center without opioid analgesic properties
Suppresses the medullary cough center through opioid analgesic activity
Reduces cough through peripheral H1 blockade with minimal CNS penetration
Reduces cough through muscarinic blockade in bronchial smooth muscle

questions.rationale: Acts on the medullary cough center to suppress cough without opioid analgesic properties. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client asks whether dextromethorphan is the same type of cough medicine as codeine. Which response is correct?

options.text: Dextromethorphan is a nonopioid antitussive
Dextromethorphan is an opioid antitussive with an analgesic effect
Dextromethorphan is a peripheral H1 blocker with a drying effect
Dextromethorphan is a muscarinic antagonist with a bronchodilator effect

questions.rationale: The prototype list identifies dextromethorphan as nonopioid and codeine as opioid.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which symptom should the nurse evaluate for improvement after prescribed dextromethorphan?

options.text: Bothersome cough frequency
Frequency of allergy-related sneezing
Severity of histamine-related itching
Intensity of acute bronchospasm

questions.rationale: Dextromethorphan suppresses the cough reflex.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client reports dizziness after dextromethorphan. Which teaching is appropriate?

options.text: Use caution with driving and activities requiring alertness
Take the next dose with food and use cough relief to judge readiness to drive
Use the normal activity schedule because dizziness is less important with a nonopioid
Switch to a nighttime dosing schedule without reviewing the prescribed interval

questions.rationale: Dizziness and drowsiness are possible even though the drug is nonopioid.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client taking dextromethorphan reports a persistent cough for more than a week and a high fever. What should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Contact the provider for evaluation
Finish another week at the labeled dose before arranging an evaluation
Change to codeine for stronger suppression before seeking an evaluation
Use the syrup more regularly and track temperature until the cough resolves

questions.rationale: The course review identifies persistent cough or high fever as reasons to seek follow-up.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which adverse effect is listed for dextromethorphan in the medication review?

options.text: Nausea or gastrointestinal upset
Dry mouth with urinary hesitancy
Palpitations with a fine tremor
White oral patches with hoarseness

questions.rationale: Gastrointestinal upset and nausea are recognized adverse effects in the review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client asks whether dextromethorphan should be used for pain relief. Which response is accurate?

options.text: It suppresses cough without providing the opioid analgesic effect of codeine
It provides mild opioid analgesia when taken at the cough-treatment dose
It provides analgesia by reducing peripheral histamine release
It provides analgesia through the same muscarinic blockade as ipratropium

questions.rationale: The course review distinguishes cough suppression from opioid analgesia.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which statement indicates that teaching about dextromethorphan was understood?

options.text: I will follow the labeled interval even if the cough returns before the next dose
I can shorten the dosing interval when symptoms return because it is nonopioid
I can judge whether to repeat a dose by the amount of cough suppression alone
I can use a second cough product without checking whether it has the same ingredient

questions.rationale: The nonopioid classification does not eliminate adverse effects or the need to follow dosing instructions.

questions.topic: Medications for the Upper Respiratory System
questions.stem: For a client prescribed Dextromethorphan, a client has both cough and sudden wheezing. Which medication distinction should the nurse reinforce?

options.text: It suppresses cough; sudden bronchospasm still needs the prescribed rescue treatment
It suppresses cough; reduced coughing is sufficient evidence that airway narrowing improved
It suppresses cough; repeating the syrup is the first step before using a rescue inhaler
It suppresses cough; its central action also provides the bronchodilation needed for wheezing

questions.rationale: Central cough suppression is different from rapid relaxation of bronchial smooth muscle.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Albuterol on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: SABA
LABA
SAMA
LAMA

questions.rationale: Albuterol is the listed prototype for SABA.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Albuterol?

options.text: Stimulates beta2 receptors to rapidly relax bronchial smooth muscle
Stimulates beta2 receptors for prolonged maintenance bronchodilation
Blocks airway muscarinic receptors to reduce bronchoconstriction
Suppresses airway immune activity to reduce mucosal edema

questions.rationale: Stimulates beta2 receptors to rapidly relax bronchial smooth muscle. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client develops sudden wheezing. Which role does prescribed albuterol have?

options.text: Rapid rescue bronchodilation
Scheduled anti-inflammatory airway control
Long-acting maintenance bronchodilation
Scheduled leukotriene-mediated prevention

questions.rationale: Albuterol is a short-acting rescue bronchodilator.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which finding after albuterol is consistent with an expected adverse effect?

options.text: Tremor and nervousness
Dry mouth and urinary hesitancy
Hoarseness and oral white patches
Constipation and blurred vision

questions.rationale: Tremor and nervousness are listed beta-agonist effects.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which measurement most directly detects the beta-adrenergic cardiac effect emphasized for albuterol?

options.text: Heart rate
Temperature
Respiratory rate
Pain intensity

questions.rationale: Albuterol can cause tachycardia and palpitations. The targeted cardiovascular effect is tachycardia or palpitations; heart rate directly assesses it.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client's wheezing decreases after albuterol. Which explanation supports this improvement?

options.text: Bronchial smooth muscle has relaxed
Airway mucosal edema has decreased through a corticosteroid effect
Acetylcholine-mediated constriction has decreased through muscarinic blockade
Leukotriene-mediated mucus production has decreased through receptor blockade

questions.rationale: Beta2 stimulation produces bronchodilation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which client statement about albuterol needs correction?

options.text: I can use albuterol on the same schedule as fluticasone because both control inflammation
I should review technique if the prescribed inhaler seems less effective
I should report a troublesome increase in pulse after treatment
I should use albuterol according to the prescribed acute-symptom plan

questions.rationale: Albuterol provides rapid bronchodilation; fluticasone reduces inflammation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client reports a pounding heartbeat after albuterol. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess the heart rate and symptoms
Review mouth-rinsing technique first because the symptom suggests local drug deposition
Assess the timing of meals first because protein commonly limits this drug's absorption
Recommend changing the next dose to bedtime before checking the current symptoms

questions.rationale: Palpitations warrant assessment because tachycardia can occur. Heart rate and the current symptoms should be assessed before changing doses or timing. Mouth rinsing and meal-protein timing do not explain this beta2-related effect.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which instruction is important for effective delivery of albuterol by metered-dose inhaler?

options.text: Check the client's demonstration of the prescribed inhaler technique
Use the degree of medication taste as the main measure of airway delivery
Check the number of actuations used without observing how the client inhales
Use the amount of visible spray escaping the mouth to judge whether delivery is adequate

questions.rationale: Correct inhaler technique helps medication reach the airways.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client must distinguish albuterol from salmeterol. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Albuterol is short acting and used for acute symptoms
Albuterol is long acting and salmeterol provides the rapid rescue effect
Albuterol blocks muscarinic receptors and salmeterol stimulates beta2 receptors
Albuterol controls airway inflammation and salmeterol relaxes airway smooth muscle

questions.rationale: Albuterol is the SABA rescue drug; salmeterol is a LABA maintenance agent.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Salmeterol on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: LABA
SABA
SAMA
LAMA

questions.rationale: Salmeterol is the listed prototype for LABA.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Salmeterol?

options.text: Produces prolonged beta2-receptor stimulation for maintenance bronchodilation
Produces rapid short-acting beta2 stimulation for rescue bronchodilation
Produces long-acting muscarinic blockade for maintenance bronchodilation
Produces local corticosteroid activity for maintenance inflammation control

questions.rationale: Produces prolonged beta2-receptor stimulation for maintenance bronchodilation. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client plans to use salmeterol for a sudden asthma attack. Which teaching is needed?

options.text: Use the prescribed rescue medicine for acute symptoms; salmeterol is maintenance therapy
Use salmeterol first for acute symptoms because its longer action prevents recurrence
Use salmeterol in place of the rescue inhaler when symptoms occur between scheduled doses
Use the next scheduled salmeterol dose early rather than follow the acute rescue plan

questions.rationale: Salmeterol is not intended to relieve acute asthma attacks.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Why is salmeterol often prescribed with an inhaled corticosteroid for asthma?

options.text: The medicines address bronchodilation and airway inflammation
Both medicines provide direct bronchodilation through different airway receptors
Both medicines suppress airway inflammation through the same receptor action
The steroid shortens salmeterol's onset so the combination becomes rescue therapy

questions.rationale: Salmeterol maintains bronchodilation while the corticosteroid treats inflammation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which adverse effect should the nurse recognize with salmeterol?

options.text: Tachycardia
Oral candidiasis
Urinary retention
Blurred vision

questions.rationale: Tachycardia is among the effects listed for salmeterol.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client feels well on maintenance salmeterol. Which statement shows understanding?

options.text: I will continue the prescribed maintenance schedule even when symptoms are controlled
I will change to as-needed use after several symptom-free days
I will use maintenance doses in place of rescue doses if wheezing recurs
I will stop the accompanying inhaled steroid once the bronchodilator is effective

questions.rationale: Maintenance therapy is scheduled according to the prescribed plan.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which medication should a client identify as the long-acting beta2 agent rather than the short-acting one?

options.text: Salmeterol
Albuterol
Ipratropium
Tiotropium

questions.rationale: Salmeterol is the LABA prototype.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client asks if salmeterol directly replaces a corticosteroid's anti-inflammatory action. Which response is best?

options.text: Its beta2 action provides maintenance bronchodilation rather than steroid anti-inflammatory action
Its beta2 action provides both the bronchodilator and corticosteroid effects
Its long duration means it can replace anti-inflammatory therapy once symptoms improve
Its long duration reflects muscarinic blockade rather than beta2 stimulation

questions.rationale: The drugs have complementary rather than identical primary actions.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which symptoms are listed as possible salmeterol effects?

options.text: Headache and muscle cramps
Dry mouth and urinary hesitancy
Hoarseness and oral white patches
Constipation and blurred vision

questions.rationale: The review lists headache, nervousness, tachycardia, and muscle cramps.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client using salmeterol reports new acute breathing difficulty. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Follow the acute rescue plan and seek help as indicated
Move the next salmeterol dose earlier and wait to see whether the symptoms settle
Use salmeterol before the rescue inhaler because longer action is preferable in an attack
Wait for the scheduled controller dose before deciding whether rescue treatment is needed

questions.rationale: Maintenance use does not eliminate the need for an acute symptom plan.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Ipratropium on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: SAMA
SABA
LABA
LAMA

questions.rationale: Ipratropium is the listed prototype for SAMA.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Ipratropium?

options.text: Blocks airway muscarinic receptors to reduce acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction
Stimulates airway beta2 receptors to provide short-acting bronchodilation
Stimulates airway beta2 receptors to provide prolonged bronchodilation
Suppresses airway inflammation through local corticosteroid activity

questions.rationale: Blocks muscarinic acetylcholine receptors in airway smooth muscle to inhibit bronchoconstriction. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which common complaint is consistent with inhaled ipratropium?

options.text: Dry mouth
Fine hand tremor
New oral white patches
Marked nervousness

questions.rationale: Dry mouth is a common anticholinergic effect.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client is prescribed both ipratropium and albuterol. Why might they be used together?

options.text: They produce bronchodilation through different receptor actions
They both stimulate beta2 receptors, increasing the duration of the same action
They both block muscarinic receptors, increasing the strength of the same action
One suppresses airway inflammation while the other suppresses the central cough reflex

questions.rationale: Different mechanisms can provide complementary bronchodilation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client reports a bitter taste after ipratropium. Which teaching matches the course review?

options.text: Rinse the mouth after use
Take the next dose with a meal to reduce systemic gastrointestinal irritation
Use a sugar-containing drink before inhalation to change the drug's airway absorption
Increase the next inhaled dose to reduce the amount remaining in the mouth

questions.rationale: The review recommends rinsing after use to reduce the bitter taste.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which finding should be evaluated as a possible local effect of ipratropium?

options.text: Throat irritation and hoarseness
White oral patches and a sore mouth
Fine hand tremor and palpitations
New vivid dreams and mood changes

questions.rationale: Throat irritation and hoarseness are listed effects.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which comparison correctly distinguishes ipratropium from tiotropium?

options.text: Ipratropium is short acting; tiotropium is long acting
Ipratropium is long acting; tiotropium is short acting
Ipratropium stimulates beta2 receptors; tiotropium blocks muscarinic receptors
Ipratropium blocks H1 receptors; tiotropium blocks leukotriene receptors

questions.rationale: The prototype document identifies SAMA and LAMA agents separately.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: For a client prescribed Ipratropium, a client asks what muscarinic blockade does in the airways. Which response is accurate?

options.text: It reduces acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction
It reduces airway inflammation by suppressing the local immune response
It reduces bronchoconstriction by stimulating beta2 receptors
It reduces mucus production by blocking leukotriene receptors

questions.rationale: Ipratropium opposes muscarinic effects that narrow the airways.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which response best suggests the intended effect of ipratropium?

options.text: Improved airflow from reduced bronchoconstriction
Reduced sneezing from peripheral H1 blockade
Reduced airway edema from local immune suppression
Reduced cough frequency from medullary suppression

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client says dry mouth means ipratropium is treating allergies by blocking H1 receptors. What needs clarification?

options.text: Dry mouth reflects muscarinic blockade; the airway target differs from an antihistamine's
Dry mouth reflects H1 blockade; ipratropium belongs to the antihistamine class
Dry mouth reflects beta2 stimulation; ipratropium belongs to the same class as albuterol
Dry mouth reflects leukotriene blockade; ipratropium belongs to the same class as montelukast

options.text: LAMA
SAMA
LABA
SABA

questions.rationale: Tiotropium is the listed prototype for LAMA.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Tiotropium?

options.text: Provides long-acting muscarinic receptor blockade for maintenance airway treatment
Provides short-acting muscarinic blockade for a shorter airway effect
Provides prolonged beta2 stimulation for maintenance bronchodilation
Provides leukotriene blockade for long-term airway inflammation control

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client receives a tiotropium inhalation capsule for the prescribed device. Which instruction is essential?

options.text: Use the capsule with its prescribed inhalation device rather than swallowing it
Swallow the capsule with water and use the device when acute wheezing develops
Open the capsule into a drink so the powder can be absorbed with the scheduled dose
Use the capsule in the albuterol inhaler because both deliver bronchodilators

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client with an enlarged prostate starts tiotropium. Which function warrants monitoring?

options.text: Ability to urinate
Appetite pattern
Sleep pattern
Bowel movement frequency

questions.rationale: Tiotropium can cause urinary retention, especially relevant with BPH.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which complaint is consistent with tiotropium's antimuscarinic effects?

options.text: Constipation and dry mouth
Tremor and palpitations
Hoarseness and oral white patches
Vivid dreams and mood changes

questions.rationale: Dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention are listed effects.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client asks whether tiotropium should replace the rescue inhaler during sudden wheezing. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: It provides maintenance treatment; use the prescribed rescue plan for sudden symptoms
Its long action makes it preferable to albuterol for initial relief of sudden symptoms
Its muscarinic blockade replaces the need for a separate acute-symptom plan
Its daily capsule can be repeated between doses when a sudden attack develops

questions.rationale: Tiotropium is a long-acting maintenance antimuscarinic.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which client statement about tiotropium shows understanding?

options.text: I will use the prescribed device and scheduled maintenance plan
I will swallow the capsule on quiet days and inhale it on symptomatic days
I will reserve the daily inhalation capsule for times when wheezing is severe
I will use the capsule with whichever inhaler device is available that morning

questions.rationale: Device-specific technique and scheduled use support maintenance therapy.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client taking tiotropium reports new difficulty voiding. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess and report possible urinary retention
Encourage less fluid intake and reassess at the next scheduled visit
Treat the symptom as a beta2 effect and review pulse monitoring first
Use mouth rinsing as the main intervention for systemic urinary symptoms

questions.rationale: Muscarinic blockade can worsen urinary retention.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which drug type best explains tiotropium's prolonged action compared with ipratropium?

options.text: Long-acting muscarinic antagonist
Short-acting muscarinic antagonist
Long-acting beta2 agonist
Leukotriene receptor antagonist

questions.rationale: Tiotropium is the LAMA prototype, unlike short-acting ipratropium.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which outcome is most consistent with effective maintenance tiotropium treatment?

options.text: Better ongoing airflow control with correct device use
Prompt relief of each acute attack after an extra maintenance capsule
Reduced oral dryness as evidence of increased muscarinic activity
Reduced airway edema through the same action as inhaled corticosteroids

questions.rationale: Maintenance bronchodilation improves ongoing airflow rather than curing infection.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: The nurse reviews Fluticasone on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroid
Leukotriene receptor antagonist
Long-acting beta2 agonist
Long-acting muscarinic antagonist

Blocks leukotriene receptors to reduce mucus production and inflammation

Blocks muscarinic receptors to reduce acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction

Rinse and swallow so the remaining steroid contributes to the treatment
Rinse before inhalation and leave the mouth unrinsed after the dose
Use a drink with the dose instead of a rinse after inhalation

Antimuscarinic dry mouth
Gingival hyperplasia
Medication-related bitter taste

questions.rationale: Thrush is a recognized local inhaled corticosteroid complication.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client has sudden wheezing and reaches for fluticasone alone. Which correction is needed?

options.text: It provides inflammation control; follow the rescue plan for immediate bronchospasm relief
It provides inflammation control; repeat its dose before considering the rescue inhaler
It provides rapid bronchodilation; use it first when acute wheezing starts
It provides both actions; wait for its full effect before following the rescue plan

questions.rationale: Fluticasone does not provide the immediate beta2 rescue action of albuterol.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client uses a bronchodilator and fluticasone at the same scheduled treatment. Which sequence matches the course review?

options.text: Bronchodilator before the corticosteroid
Corticosteroid before the bronchodilator
Alternate the sequence with each scheduled treatment
Use the corticosteroid first when wheezing is present

questions.stem: Which finding is a listed local effect of fluticasone?

Fine tremor
Urinary hesitancy
Vivid dreams

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which statement shows understanding of maintenance fluticasone?

options.text: I will follow the regular plan even when I am not acutely wheezing
I will change to as-needed use after several days without wheezing
I will use it primarily before exercise instead of following the maintenance schedule
I will stop maintenance doses once the bronchodilator starts improving airflow

questions.rationale: Controller therapy treats underlying inflammation and should follow the prescribed schedule.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Why should the nurse evaluate inhaler technique in a client taking fluticasone?

options.text: Poor technique reduces lung delivery and can leave more medication in the mouth
Poor technique converts its local anti-inflammatory action into rapid bronchodilation
Poor technique changes it from a corticosteroid into a muscarinic antagonist
Poor technique is compensated for by swallowing the medicine deposited in the mouth

questions.rationale: Appropriate inhaler technique supports lung delivery and limits avoidable local exposure. Technique affects deposition and airway delivery; it does not change the drug class or make swallowed residue a substitute for correct inhalation.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client asks why fluticasone and salmeterol may both be prescribed. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: They address airway inflammation and maintenance bronchodilation
They provide short-acting and long-acting beta2 stimulation
They provide short-acting and long-acting muscarinic blockade
They provide two routes for the same leukotriene-blocking action

questions.rationale: The combination addresses different components of airway disease.

Inhaled corticosteroid

Long-acting muscarinic antagonist

Suppresses airway immune responses directly to reduce edema and inflammation
Stimulates beta2 receptors to reduce airway resistance and improve airflow
Blocks muscarinic receptors to reduce acetylcholine-mediated bronchoconstriction

Hoarseness after an inhaled corticosteroid

In the morning with the first meal as the asthma schedule
At midday with the largest meal as the asthma schedule
At the onset of wheezing instead of a regular evening dose

questions.rationale: The course review lists once-daily evening use for asthma protection.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A client plans to use montelukast instead of a rescue inhaler during acute wheezing. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Montelukast is not for acute exacerbation relief
Montelukast should be taken first because its oral route reaches all airways
Montelukast should be repeated once before moving to the rescue inhaler
Montelukast provides the same acute bronchodilation as a short-acting beta2 agonist

questions.rationale: The in-class source distinguishes controller use from acute rescue treatment.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which assessment should be part of montelukast follow-up?

options.text: Changes in behavior, mood, or sleep experiences
Gum enlargement and dental bleeding
Urinary hesitancy and bowel slowing
Tremor and pulse changes after inhaled doses

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: A family reports new vivid dreams after montelukast was started. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Evaluate the change and contact the prescriber as appropriate
Treat the dreams as an expected sign of improved sleep and continue routine follow-up
Change the dose to morning independently and review the dreams at the next refill
Take the dose with food and wait for the dreams to resolve before reporting them

questions.rationale: Vivid dreams are included among possible neuropsychiatric events.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which effect supports montelukast's role in long-term airway care?

options.text: Reduced leukotriene-mediated inflammation and mucus
Rapid relaxation of airway smooth muscle through beta2 stimulation
Reduced acetylcholine-mediated airway constriction through muscarinic blockade
Reduced immune activity in the airways through corticosteroid receptor effects

Oral candidiasis

My family and I will judge safety mainly by whether breathing symptoms improve
My family and I will wait until the next refill to mention disturbing new dreams
My family and I will change the dosing time ourselves if behavior changes occur

questions.rationale: Neuropsychiatric monitoring is an important part of montelukast teaching.

Dopaminergic agent

Enhances GABA activity by binding to benzodiazepine receptors

Increases cerebral acetylcholine by inhibiting its breakdown

Reduced frequency of medication-related involuntary movements

Improved recall of a familiar daily routine

Insomnia and increased appetite

Muscle rigidity and slowed movement

Use it on alternate days without a dose review once symptoms are controlled
Keep the same dose but take it only on days when the pain returns
Finish the current supply and stop without reviewing the discontinuation schedule

New oral white patches
New urinary hesitancy

Schedule routine independent walking after each dose to establish tolerance
Move the next dose to bedtime independently and resume usual activity
Use improvement in pain, rather than balance, to decide whether help is needed

questions.rationale: Dizziness and somnolence can impair balance and safety.

options.text: Its structural similarity to GABA means it works by binding benzodiazepine receptors
Its calcium-channel effects can reduce excitatory neurotransmitter release
Its effects can include dizziness and daytime sleepiness
Its discontinuation plan should be reviewed rather than changed abruptly

questions.rationale: Gabapentin is not dopamine replacement; it modulates calcium-channel-related neurotransmitter release. Structural similarity to GABA does not make gabapentin a benzodiazepine receptor agonist; the review describes calcium-channel modulation.

questions.stem: Which behavioral change warrants follow-up in a client taking gabapentin?

options.text: Worsening depression or suicidal thoughts
Reduced burning discomfort after the prescribed dose
Mild sleepiness shortly after the prescribed dose
A request to review the planned discontinuation schedule

questions.rationale: The review recommends monitoring for worsening depression or suicidal behavior.

questions.stem: Which assessment is important before a client taking gabapentin resumes driving?

options.text: How dizziness and sleepiness affect alertness
Whether pain relief lasts through the planned drive
Whether the client took the medication with the last meal
Whether peripheral swelling is unchanged since the last visit

questions.rationale: CNS effects may impair safe driving even when pain improves.

GABA analog
CNS stimulant

Carbidopa becomes cerebral dopamine; levodopa limits its peripheral breakdown
Levodopa blocks cerebral dopamine receptors; carbidopa limits its adverse effects
Carbidopa increases cerebral acetylcholine; levodopa slows acetylcholine breakdown

Alzheimer disease
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder
Generalized anxiety disorder

It prevents levodopa from crossing the blood-brain barrier until the next dose
It blocks cerebral dopamine receptors to reduce levodopa's motor effects
It converts peripheral acetylcholine into the dopamine needed in the brain

Medication-related dyskinesia
End-of-dose wearing off
Anticholinergic urinary retention

Take it with a high-protein meal to increase transport into the brain
Judge meal timing by tyramine content rather than protein content
Increase protein intake near the dose to slow peripheral levodopa breakdown

An involuntary dyskinesia occurring near the medication's strongest effect
An orthostatic episode associated specifically with standing
A benign pigment change associated with levodopa metabolism

questions.rationale: The review describes wearing-off near the end of dosing cycles. End-of-dose recurrence distinguishes wearing off from involuntary movements at other points in the dosing cycle and positional dizziness.

questions.stem: Which movement change may be an adverse effect of carbidopa-levodopa?

options.text: Involuntary dyskinesias
Reduced tremor during routine activities
Improved initiation of a voluntary movement
Return of stiffness before the next dose

questions.rationale: Dyskinesias are listed adverse effects and should be distinguished from treatment goals.

questions.stem: A client is alarmed by dark sweat or urine while taking carbidopa-levodopa. Which explanation matches the review?

Dark sweat or urine is evidence of wearing off and needs a shorter dose interval
Dark sweat or urine is evidence of reduced absorption and needs a high-protein meal

questions.stem: Which client plan helps reduce injury risk during carbidopa-levodopa therapy?

Stand promptly after the dose so the medication has time to improve movement
Use reduced stiffness as the main guide to safe transfers even when lightheaded
Take each dose with a high-protein snack to prevent positional dizziness

questions.rationale: Slow position changes address orthostatic symptoms and fall risk.

Benzodiazepine

Modulates calcium channels to decrease excitatory transmitter release

Inhibits acetylcholinesterase to increase synaptic acetylcholine

Amylase and lipase
Fasting glucose and lipid concentrations

Oral candidiasis
Anticholinergic dry mouth
Local inhaler-related irritation

Reduce brushing around enlarged gums and defer dental care until treatment ends

Document the rash as a routine effect and discuss it at the next scheduled visit
Treat the rash as a localized contact effect and continue the usual monitoring plan

Restlessness and an inability to remain seated
Repetitive lip smacking and tongue movements
Fine hand tremor and increased urination

Previous mild oral dryness with an inhaled medicine
Previous short-lived nausea with a cough suppressant
Previous mild insomnia with a daytime allergy medicine

questions.rationale: The course review identifies teratogenicity as an important phenytoin concern.

Use seizure frequency to decide whether the next blood draw can be deferred
Replace concentration monitoring with gum checks while seizure control is stable
Resume concentration monitoring only if a new breakthrough seizure occurs

Reduced involuntary movements associated with dopamine replacement
Improved attention during an age-appropriate school task
Improved recall of familiar people and activities

questions.rationale: The treatment goal is seizure control; the other findings are adverse effects.

Benzodiazepine

Enhances GABA inhibition mainly by binding benzodiazepine receptors
Modulates calcium channels to reduce excitatory transmitter release
Inhibits acetylcholinesterase to increase synaptic acetylcholine

Thrombocytopenia
Anticholinergic activity

Serum amylase and lipase
CBC with platelet count
Serum creatinine and thyroid studies

Peripheral edema
Anticholinergic urinary retention

Liver enzymes and bilirubin
CBC with platelet count
Fasting glucose and lipid panel

Reduced thyroid activity
Increased cholinergic activity

Amylase and lipase
Renal panel with creatinine

Improved seizure control on the prescribed schedule

Valproic acid

Increased alertness with reduced appetite

Repetitive movements with muscle rigidity

Change to every-other-day dosing without review once anxiety improves

questions.rationale: Alters ion transport and neurotransmitter signaling in nerve and muscle cells. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.stem: Which teaching is central to lithium safety?

options.text: Maintain consistent sodium intake and the prescribed adequate fluid intake
Reduce sodium intake progressively while keeping the same lithium dose
Reduce fluid intake when urination increases while keeping the same dose
Match lithium doses to the amount of sodium eaten at each meal

questions.rationale: The Jeopardy and review emphasize stable sodium and fluid balance.

questions.stem: A client taking lithium has vomiting, diarrhea, and new neurologic changes. Which concern has priority?

options.text: Possible lithium toxicity
An expected fine hand tremor without new symptoms
Anticholinergic bowel slowing without new symptoms
A routine local medication effect without new symptoms

questions.rationale: The in-class review emphasizes GI plus neurologic symptoms as a toxicity warning.

questions.stem: Which laboratory measurement directly checks whether lithium is within its prescribed therapeutic concentration range?

options.text: Ordered serum lithium concentrations
Fasting blood glucose and lipid concentrations
Serum amylase and lipase concentrations
CBC with platelet count

questions.rationale: Serum concentration monitoring is important because the therapeutic range is narrow.

questions.stem: A client taking lithium wants to start an NSAID without consultation. Which response is appropriate?

options.text: Review it with the prescriber because an NSAID may increase lithium concentrations
Separate the NSAID and lithium by an hour to prevent a concentration increase
Take the NSAID with food to prevent an effect on lithium concentrations
Use symptom control to decide whether an interaction review is needed

questions.rationale: The review warns that NSAIDs can increase lithium exposure. Taking the NSAID with food or at a different time does not establish that the lithium interaction is prevented.

questions.stem: Which organ functions require attention during lithium therapy?

options.text: Renal and thyroid function
Hepatic and pancreatic function
Hematologic and coagulation function
Pulmonary and upper-airway function

questions.rationale: Renal impairment and hypothyroidism are listed lithium concerns.

questions.stem: A client taking lithium starts a diuretic. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review the interaction and monitoring plan with the prescriber
Separate administration times and keep the same lithium monitoring plan
Use the increase in urine output as evidence of protection against lithium toxicity
Reduce fluid intake to compensate for the diuretic before discussing the interaction

questions.rationale: Diuretics can affect lithium levels and require individualized review. A timing change or greater urine output does not establish safety; the interaction and monitoring plan need review.

questions.stem: Which finding is listed as a possible lithium effect?

options.text: Fine hand tremor and increased urination
Gum enlargement and ataxia
Slow pulse and diarrhea
Urinary hesitancy and oral dryness

questions.rationale: Fine tremor and polyuria are listed; worsening or additional symptoms need evaluation.

questions.stem: A client taking lithium plans strenuous activity in hot weather. Which teaching is relevant?

options.text: Review hydration and the prescribed sodium plan before prolonged activity in heat
Replace sweat losses with plain water while sharply reducing dietary sodium
Reduce fluids during activity to offset lithium-related increased urination
Use extra lithium after heavy sweating to compensate for the fluid loss

questions.rationale: Changes in fluid and sodium balance can increase toxicity risk.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews Chlorpromazine on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: First-generation antipsychotic
Second-generation antipsychotic
Tricyclic antidepressant
Mood stabilizer

questions.rationale: Chlorpromazine is the listed prototype for First-generation antipsychotic.

questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Chlorpromazine?

options.text: Blocks central dopamine D2 receptors and has anticholinergic activity
Blocks serotonin 5-HT2 and dopamine D2 receptors as an atypical antipsychotic
Inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake as a tricyclic antidepressant
Increases cerebral dopamine through conversion of a dopamine precursor

questions.rationale: Blocks central dopamine D2 receptors and has anticholinergic activity. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.stem: A client taking chlorpromazine develops fever, severe muscle rigidity, and autonomic instability. Which emergency should be considered?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Serotonin syndrome
Acute dystonia
Tardive dyskinesia

questions.rationale: The Jeopardy and review emphasize this NMS warning cluster. The antipsychotic exposure with severe rigidity, fever, and autonomic instability raises concern for NMS; the other movement syndromes do not by themselves explain that systemic emergency.

questions.stem: A client taking chlorpromazine develops repetitive lip smacking and tongue movements. Which adverse effect fits?

options.text: Tardive dyskinesia
Akathisia
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Acute dystonia

questions.rationale: These involuntary movements are characteristic of tardive dyskinesia. Repetitive lip and tongue movements fit tardive dyskinesia. Akathisia is restlessness, and dystonia involves sustained abnormal contractions.

questions.stem: Which conduction change is specifically emphasized for chlorpromazine in the course review?

options.text: Prolonged QT interval
Sinus tachycardia from beta2-receptor stimulation
Bradycardia from acetylcholinesterase inhibition
Hypertension from norepinephrine reuptake inhibition

questions.rationale: The review identifies QT prolongation as a safety issue.

questions.stem: A client taking chlorpromazine reports restlessness and an inability to sit still. Which type of effect should the nurse assess?

options.text: Extrapyramidal symptoms such as akathisia
Tardive dyskinesia with repetitive oral movements
Drug-induced parkinsonism with slowed movement
Acute dystonia with sustained abnormal muscle contractions

questions.rationale: Akathisia is among the EPS manifestations identified for monitoring.

questions.stem: Which symptom cluster during chlorpromazine therapy requires urgent rather than routine follow-up?

options.text: High fever, rigidity, and altered mental status
Dry mouth and mild constipation without systemic symptoms
Restlessness and difficulty sitting still without fever
Repetitive oral movements without an acute systemic change

questions.rationale: The cluster may indicate NMS, a rare emergency. The acute systemic cluster raises concern for NMS. Nonfebrile movement changes also need assessment, but they do not match this emergency cluster.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates a client taking chlorpromazine for new abnormal movements. Which assessment belongs in this evaluation?

options.text: Dystonia, parkinsonism, or tardive movements
Appetite, body weight, and fasting glucose trends
Bowel frequency, oral moisture, and urinary hesitancy
Sleep pattern, daytime sedation, and meal timing

questions.rationale: The review recommends monitoring several extrapyramidal syndromes.

questions.stem: Which receptor effect helps explain chlorpromazine-related dry mouth or constipation?

options.text: Muscarinic blockade
Dopamine D2 blockade
Serotonin 5-HT2 blockade
Alpha-adrenergic blockade

questions.rationale: The review notes significant anticholinergic properties.

questions.stem: Which client statement about chlorpromazine requires correction?

options.text: I can wait until my next visit to report fever and severe stiffness if psychiatric symptoms are controlled
I should report new tongue or facial movements even if I feel emotionally better
I should keep recommended cardiac monitoring despite improved symptoms
I should discuss troublesome dry mouth or constipation during treatment

questions.rationale: Possible NMS symptoms require prompt evaluation regardless of psychiatric improvement.

questions.stem: The nurse reviews Risperidone on a medication list. Which drug class should the nurse identify?

options.text: Second-generation antipsychotic
First-generation antipsychotic
Mood stabilizer
Tricyclic antidepressant

questions.rationale: Risperidone is the listed prototype for Second-generation antipsychotic.

questions.stem: Which action explains the therapeutic effect of Risperidone?

options.text: Blocks serotonin 5-HT2 and dopamine D2 receptors
Primarily blocks dopamine D2 receptors with the typical antipsychotic profile
Inhibits serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake with a TCA receptor profile
Inhibits norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake with an NDRI profile

questions.rationale: Blocks serotonin 5-HT2 and dopamine D2 receptors. This is the action described in the course medication review.

questions.stem: A client taking risperidone develops weight gain and hyperglycemia. Which condition should the nurse consider?

options.text: Metabolic syndrome
Extrapyramidal symptoms
Hyperprolactinemia
Anticholinergic adverse effects

questions.rationale: The Jeopardy identifies metabolic syndrome with this pattern.

questions.stem: Which measurements target the metabolic adverse effects associated with risperidone?

options.text: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipid levels
Serum lithium, creatinine, and thyroid studies
Liver enzymes, amylase, and platelet count
Serum phenytoin concentration and dental assessment

questions.rationale: The review recommends metabolic monitoring. These measurements address metabolic risk. The other grouped assessments address lithium, valproic acid, or phenytoin safety.

questions.stem: A client taking risperidone says a lower EPS risk means abnormal movements cannot occur. Which response is correct?

options.text: The risk is lower than with typical agents, but movement symptoms still need assessment
The risk is lower, so assess movement only when the metabolic panel changes
The risk is lower, so improved psychiatric symptoms replace movement screening
The risk is lower, so motor slowing should be treated as a therapeutic response

questions.rationale: The review describes lower rather than absent EPS risk.

questions.stem: Which teaching helps address risperidone's metabolic risks?

options.text: Discuss healthy eating, activity, and scheduled metabolic checks
Use appetite changes alone to decide whether metabolic blood tests are needed
Focus on weight checks and defer glucose testing when the weight is stable
Use a normal initial glucose result to decide whether future lipid tests are needed

questions.rationale: Lifestyle measures and monitoring address metabolic concerns.

questions.stem: Which laboratory change is associated with risperidone in the review?

options.text: Elevated prolactin
Elevated amylase
Reduced platelet count
Elevated serum lithium

questions.rationale: Hyperprolactinemia is a listed risperidone effect. Prolactin is distinct from pancreatic enzymes, platelet counts, and lithium concentrations.

questions.stem: A client gains substantial weight after starting risperidone. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess the trend and review metabolic monitoring and the treatment plan
Use improved psychiatric symptoms as the main reason to defer metabolic review
Address diet alone and wait for weight loss before ordering metabolic follow-up
Wait for abnormal movements before discussing the weight trend with the prescriber

questions.rationale: Weight gain is a relevant metabolic adverse effect.

questions.stem: Which finding is more consistent with a metabolic than an extrapyramidal effect of risperidone?

options.text: Increased fasting blood glucose
New repetitive tongue movements
New rigidity with motor slowing
A new inability to sit still

questions.rationale: Hyperglycemia is metabolic; the other options describe movement effects.

questions.stem: Which statement about risperidone requires correction?

options.text: Stable weight means I can defer glucose and lipid checks while symptoms stay controlled
I should discuss new stiffness or repetitive movements despite improved mood
I should keep the scheduled weight checks while taking the medicine
I should discuss eating and activity habits as part of the treatment plan

questions.rationale: Psychiatric benefit does not remove the need for metabolic safety monitoring. Stable weight and controlled psychiatric symptoms do not substitute for the planned glucose and lipid monitoring.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which findings match the adverse-effect profile emphasized for albuterol? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tachycardia
Fine hand tremor
Nervousness
Palpitations
Oral white patches
Urinary hesitancy

questions.rationale: Albuterol can cause tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, and nervousness. Oral candidiasis is a local inhaled-corticosteroid concern; urinary hesitancy is associated with antimuscarinic effects.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which instructions support correct prescribed inhaled fluticasone use? Select all that apply.

options.text: Rinse the mouth and spit out the rinse after inhalation
Continue the prescribed maintenance schedule when symptoms are controlled
Report new white patches inside the mouth
Use the dose primarily when wheezing begins rather than on the maintenance schedule
Take it before the bronchodilator when both are scheduled together
Swallow the mouth rinse to improve the airway dose

questions.rationale: Rinsing and spitting limits local exposure, regular use provides maintenance inflammation control, and oral white patches need assessment for candidiasis. The course review places the bronchodilator before fluticasone when both are scheduled together. Swallowing residue does not replace airway delivery.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which new findings match the neuropsychiatric warning emphasized for montelukast? Select all that apply.

options.text: Suicidal thoughts
Marked mood change
New disturbing vivid dreams
Difficulty emptying the bladder
Fine tremor immediately after a rescue inhaler

questions.rationale: The course warning includes suicidal thoughts, mood or behavior changes, and vivid dreams. Urinary retention resembles an antimuscarinic effect; post-rescue-inhaler tremor resembles a beta2-agonist effect rather than this neuropsychiatric warning.

questions.topic: Medications for the Lower Respiratory System
questions.stem: Which findings match the antimuscarinic adverse effects listed for tiotropium? Select all that apply.

options.text: Dry mouth
Constipation
Urinary retention
Oral candidiasis
Gingival overgrowth
Fine hand tremor after inhalation

questions.rationale: Tiotropium's listed antimuscarinic effects include dry mouth, constipation, and urinary retention. The alternatives resemble inhaled corticosteroid, phenytoin, or beta2-agonist concerns.

questions.stem: Which plans match the safety teaching emphasized for phenytoin? Select all that apply.

options.text: Obtain serum drug concentrations as ordered
Maintain regular dental care and oral hygiene
Promptly report a severe new skin rash
Discuss pregnancy or pregnancy plans with the prescriber
Use seizure-free days to decide when a blood draw can be deferred
Replace dental follow-up with mouth rinsing if gum enlargement occurs

questions.rationale: The review emphasizes serum concentrations, oral hygiene and dental cleanings, severe-rash monitoring, and teratogenic risk. Seizure control does not establish a safe concentration, and rinsing alone does not replace dental care.

questions.stem: Which findings suggest the serious hepatic, pancreatic, or hematologic effects emphasized for valproic acid? Select all that apply.

options.text: Yellowing skin or eyes
Significant new abdominal pain
Unusual bruising
Isolated mild dry mouth
Isolated mild hoarseness after an inhaled medicine

questions.rationale: Jaundice, significant abdominal pain, and unusual bruising raise concern for hepatotoxicity, pancreatitis, and thrombocytopenia. The isolated local symptoms do not match these specified organ or hematologic warning patterns.

questions.stem: Which concerns are emphasized for lorazepam treatment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Respiratory depression
Sedation
Physical dependence with regular use
Tolerance with repeated use
Cholinergic diarrhea with bradycardia
Gingival enlargement with dental bleeding

questions.rationale: Lorazepam can cause CNS and respiratory depression, tolerance, and physical dependence. The other patterns resemble donepezil and phenytoin effects rather than the benzodiazepine profile listed in the review.

questions.stem: Which assessments target the growth and cardiovascular effects emphasized for a child taking methylphenidate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Appetite, height, weight, and growth trend
Resting heart rate and blood pressure
Fasting glucose and lipid panel
Serum drug concentration and gum enlargement
Thyroid studies and renal function

questions.rationale: Methylphenidate monitoring targets appetite suppression, weight/growth changes, tachycardia, and hypertension. The other assessment groups correspond to antipsychotic metabolic risk, phenytoin monitoring, or lithium monitoring, rather than these specified stimulant effects.

questions.stem: Which findings match the serotonin-syndrome warning emphasized for fluoxetine? Select all that apply.

options.text: Fever
Agitation or altered mental status
Hyperreflexia
Tremor
Isolated constipation
Isolated urinary hesitancy

questions.rationale: The review describes fever, tremor, hyperreflexia, and agitation with serotonin syndrome. Isolated constipation and urinary hesitancy resemble anticholinergic effects rather than the specified serotonergic warning pattern.

questions.stem: Which plans support safe lithium treatment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Maintain consistent sodium intake and the prescribed adequate fluid intake
Obtain serum lithium concentrations as ordered
Reduce dietary sodium when increased urination occurs
Try an NSAID for a week before asking about its interaction
Separate the diuretic and lithium doses instead of reviewing the interaction

questions.rationale: A stable sodium/fluid plan and ordered serum levels support lithium safety. Sodium depletion can increase toxicity risk; NSAIDs and diuretics require interaction review rather than a trial period or a timing workaround.

questions.stem: Which findings raise concern for NMS during chlorpromazine treatment? Select all that apply.

options.text: High fever
Severe muscle rigidity
Autonomic instability
Restlessness without fever or a systemic change
Repetitive lip movements without an acute systemic change

questions.rationale: NMS is associated with high fever, severe rigidity, altered mental status, and autonomic instability. Isolated restlessness or repetitive oral movements can represent other extrapyramidal effects that still need assessment, but they do not by themselves match the NMS cluster.

questions.stem: Which measurements specifically target risperidone-associated metabolic risk? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weight trend
Fasting blood glucose
Lipid panel
Serum prolactin
QT interval
Assessment for abnormal involuntary movements

questions.rationale: Weight, fasting glucose, and lipids monitor metabolic effects. Prolactin, cardiac conduction, and movement assessments address different adverse-effect domains rather than the specified metabolic risk.
